newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World steel market hit by oversupply, UN says.
newsitem.headline: World steel market hit by oversupply, UN says.

text.p: The world steel market, confronted by a large expansion of new crude steel-making capacity in North America and Asia, is threatened by oversupply in the period to 1999, a new United Nations study said on Tuesday.
The Russian Federation and the Ukraine also have huge output overcapacity which will require major funds to restructure, according to the U.N. Economic Commission for Europe (ECE).

"The 1997 world steel market is expected to show somewhat favourable trends. However, it should be recognised that the world steel market is fragile and threatened by concerns about oversupply in the short term and the potential for an overcapacity build-up in the medium term," it said.
"An effort to avoid an over-supply situation and to match supply to the level which the market requires is essential."

The annual study, "The Steel Market in 1996 and Prospects for 1997", said global crude steel production reached 748 million metric tonnes in 1996, a drop of 0.3 per cent from 1995. The 173-page report gave no forecast for 1997.
China overtook Japan as the largest steel producer for the first time last year -- the only country to exceed the 100 million tonne level, according to the Geneva-based ECE.

It attributed the overall global decline mainly to stock reductions and weakening economic activity in the European Union countries and Japan, which continued their adjustment for high levels of inventory from the end of 1995 through 1996.
The study, written by Japanese staff economist Akio Noguchi, predicted total new crude steel-making capacity in North America and Asia will grow by 12 million tonnes to 87.7 million in 1997.
Out of the 87.7 million tonne rise, new electronic arc furnace capacity is expected to reach up to 60.3 million tonnes.
"Most increases in new capacity will take place in Asia. Strong increases in new capacity will take place particularly in Malaysia, Thailand, and the Taiwan Province of China," it said.
In last year's ECE survey, new capacity in Asia was reported as 57.5 million tonnes from 1995/96 to 1999. In the current survey, the forecast figure has risen to 70.3 million tonnes.

In South Korea, Posco is constructing no. 5 blast furnace at Kwanyang due to be completed in 1999, raising capacity by three million tonnes, it said. A mini-mill project to be completed there that year will add a further two million tonne capacity.
"The new facilities will make Posco the largest mill in the world in 1999, ahead of Nippon Steel," the ECE study said.
In the United States, five new mini-mill flat-product plants totalling 5.8 million tonnes in capacity came on stream in 1996.
"In North America, there will be no substantial increase in new capacity from that reported in the 1996 survey, i.e. it will remain at 17.4 million tonnes," the ECE study said.

"This is partially because new steel-making capacity including the conventional long product sector has developed very rapidly in recent years, and partially because the United States steel market is already matured, although apparent steel consumption has remained at a high level due to a sustained economic dynamics in recent years," the report added.
In the Russian Federation -- which became the largest steel exporting country in 1995 -- capacity utilisation is estimated at a low rate of about 67 per cent.
"Recent production overcapacity in Russia and Ukraine is estimated to be very high, amounting to approximately 20-30 million tonnes," it said.
